title: Education
levelNote: Six tiers in one file. A lesson takes the slice at or below the learner's level, so a beginner meets teacher and classroom and an advanced learner meets curriculum and plagiarism — same topic, same file, different depth.
goal: Talk about school and university life, follow classroom instructions, and hold a conversation about study.
goal_pt: Falar sobre a vida na escola e na universidade, seguir instruções de sala de aula, e manter uma conversa sobre estudos.

dialogue.title: Talking to a teacher about homework

lines.text: Excuse me, I have a question about the homework.
Of course. What is the problem?
I do not understand the second exercise.
You must read the instructions again first.
I did, but the timetable says the exam is on the same subject next week.
Then let's go through it together now.
Thank you, that would help a lot.

questions.q: What does the teacher ask A to do first?

lines.text: I would like to ask about the scholarship for this degree.
Certainly. Which faculty are you applying to?
Engineering. The tuition is quite high for my family.
The scholarship covers half the tuition for the first semester.
And after the first semester?
It depends on your grades. It was renewed for most students last year.
That is reassuring. When does the semester start?
Lectures begin in the first week of September.

reading.title: A day at school
reading.text:
Marco walks to school with his sister every morning. School starts at eight, so they leave the house early.

In the classroom, the teacher writes the date on the board. Marco opens his book and takes out his pencil. His friend sits next to him and shares a rubber.

At lunchtime they eat outside. Then the lesson starts again, and Marco tries to remember everything before the bell rings.

questions.q: Who does Marco sit next to?

reading.title: The subject I used to hate
reading.text:
I used to hate maths. Every lesson felt like the teacher was speaking a language I had not been taught, and every exam confirmed it. I told myself I was simply not a maths person, the way some people are not tall.

What changed was not the subject. It was a teacher who slowed down and let me ask the same question three times without making me feel small for it. Slowly the numbers stopped being strangers.

By the final semester I was helping classmates with the exercises I had once dreaded. I do not think I became naturally good at maths. I think I stopped believing the story I had told myself since I was eight.

questions.q: What did the writer believe about themselves?
options: That they were not a maths person

questions.q: By the final semester, what was the writer doing?

reading.title: What a grade cannot measure
reading.text:
A grade is a single number standing in for months of work, and like any summary it discards almost everything it summarises. Two students can arrive at the same mark on a dissertation by entirely different routes: one wrote a confident first draft and polished it, the other rewrote the argument four times after every meeting with a supervisor. The certificate does not record the difference.

This is not an argument against grading, which remains a genuinely useful shorthand when a university has thousands of students and needs some way to compare them. It is an argument against treating the shorthand as the whole truth. A curriculum can be followed perfectly and still leave a student unable to explain why any of it mattered, and it can be followed imperfectly by a student who understood the one idea that counted.

What a transcript is good at is comparison. What it is bad at is the thing most people actually want to know, which is not how a student performed against a syllabus but whether they can now think somewhat differently than they could before they started. That question has no grade, and probably should not.

questions.q: What does the writer say a grade discards?
What is grading useful for, according to the writer?
What question does the writer say has no grade?
options: Whether a dissertation was long enough
Whether a student attended every lecture
Whether a student can now think differently
